title: 2026-12-02 p99/p95 tail latency deep dive with Equinox Labs
summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency for Equinox's realtime chat product. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache cold misses, batching strategies, quantization trade-offs, and VPC networking hops. Agreed on pilot benchmarks and config recommendations; SE to propose dedicated pool sizes and quant profiles, AE to share benchmark sheet and pricing.

KV cache warmup and prefix caching
monitoring and tracing for tail latency

transcript:
[00:00] Samir Patel: Hey Aisha, thanks for joining. We're on for the tail latency deep dive, we've got Lena and Miguel here from infra. How's every
[00:10] Aisha Khan: Good, thanks. We ran into some p99 spikes last week on our chat product when session length jumps above 800 tokens, so excited to dig in.
[00:22] Lena Ortiz: Great. Quick agenda: measure definitions, streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching, quantization, and network hops. We'll go through traces you shared.
[00:35] Ben Cho: Quick note  we saw a big first-token gap in streaming; non-streaming seemed faster for some flows which is weird.
[00:43] Miguel Santos: That can happen if your streaming path has an extra proxy or if the runtime is block-waiting for batch formation. Also sometimes the SDK sends small chunks that prevent continuous batching.
[00:56] Speaker 1: (mumbles) the SDK has a 20ms flush by default, I think.
[01:02] Lena Ortiz: Right, micro-batching flush windows are critical. If you set very small flush it increases throughput but hurts p99 because of scheduling jitter. Conversely, large flush increases latency for small sessions.
[01:18] Aisha Khan: Can you explain the KV cache cold miss story again? Our logs show huge outliers when keys are not present.
[01:26] Lena Ortiz: Sure. So KV cache is per-session prefix+KV. If a request hits a cache miss we need to recompute the KV for the prefix, which is effectively re-doing token computation and adds 60-200ms depending on model and sequence length. On multi-tenant hosted infra there can also be eviction noise if the cache is shared.
[01:45] Ben Cho: We're on a dedicated-ish plan but still see evictions when loads spike. Do we need private on-prem to avoid that?
[01:52] Samir Patel: Not necessarily. Dedicated pools with pinned capacity and appropriately sized KV partitions cut eviction substantially. Also warmup strategies  keep hot prefixes pinned, pre-warm KV for expected flows.
[02:05] Aisha Khan: What's the difference between streaming and non-streaming first-token latency in practice?
[02:10] Miguel Santos: Streaming adds a small serialization window and often an additional network hop (proxy or websocket gateway). Non-streaming batched responses can be returned once generation completes, removing the extra websocket handshake, so first token can sometimes be faster if you avoid stream overhead. But streaming improves perceived latency for users because they see tokens earlier.
[02:30] Ben Cho: Example  we saw p95 ~ 120ms but p99 at 420ms; first token streaming p95 was 140ms and p99 520ms.
[02:39] Lena Ortiz: Those numbers are consistent with cold cache and network jitter. Have you correlated p99 events with sequence length and cache hit rate?
[02:46] Aisha Khan: Partially  long sessions correlate, plus a subset that come through mobile region over a NAT.
[02:53] Miguel Santos: NATs and additional hops introduce tail jitter. If requests traverse customer VPC -> NAT -> Redwood edge -> regional proxy -> runtime, each hop adds variance. We typically recommend reducing hops for latency-sensitive apps: VPC peering or dedicated interconnects when possible.
[03:10] Speaker 1: (interrupting) are there logs that show hop counts?
[03:13] Lena Ortiz: Yes, our tracing includes path metadata if you enable the network trace flag. We'll share an example trace.
[03:20] Samir Patel: On quantization  moving from fp16 to int8 gives latency wins on kernel runtime but can sometimes increase generation steps (slight quality degradation) requiring more tokens/refixes. So tradeoffs exist: int8 often reduces per-token latency by 10-25% on some GPUs, but you must validate against your eval prompts.
[03:42] Aisha Khan: Is int8 safe for our summarization flows? We care about semantic fidelity more than a few percentage points of throughput.
[03:48] Lena Ortiz: Run an eval harness  we can provide the Redwood optimize config and recommended quant profiles per model. For summary workloads we often suggest q4_0 or quantization knobs that keep attention stable.
[03:58] Ben Cho: What about batching? We run mixed workloads: short replies (20-40 tokens) interleaved with long generations (800-1200). How to batch without hurting short flows?
[04:10] Miguel Santos: Continuous batching with dynamic shaping helps. You can prioritize short requests into smaller sub-pools and route long sessions to dedicated instances or pre-warmed KV lanes. Also prefix caching helps because if prefixes are hot you avoid recompute and batch windows shrink.
[04:26] Aisha Khan: Can we pin model variants for critical routes?
[04:29] Samir Patel: Yes  Redwood routing allows pinning to model variants and capacity tiers. For p99-sensitive routes we recommend pinning to a dedicated pool with pre-warmed KV and lower maximum batch size to limit serialization jitter.
[04:41] Ben Cho: We noticed p99 spikes around autoscale events. Any recommendations?
[04:46] Lena Ortiz: Autoscaling adds variability  cold-start allocation and load redistribution cause transient p99s. Solutions: buffer with burst capacity, use warm standby instances, and run graceful drain with overprovisioning. For Dedicated you can configure minimum pool size and scale buffers.
[05:01] Aisha Khan: For our pilot, what config should we try?
[05:04] Lena Ortiz: Proposal: a dedicated pool equivalent to 4x A10-class GPUs, continuous batching with per-route micro-batch timeout=10ms, KV partitions sized to avoid eviction for your session count (we'll calculate), int8 quant profile for lower-latency model variant, and network peer to reduce NAT hops. We'll send detailed numbers.
[05:21] Miguel Santos: Also instrument traces for prefix-level cache hit rate and per-token kernel timings. That helps diagnose whether it's kernel compute, scheduling, or network.
[05:32] Ben Cho: Can you share the benchmark sheet and example traces?
[05:35] Samir Patel: Yup, I'll drop the benchmark sheet and a short how-to for collecting traces. Link will be in the follow-up.
[05:42] Aisha Khan: Security question  if we peer via VPC do we lose audit visibility? We need full request audit logs for compliance.
[05:50] Samir Patel: No, logs are preserved. In Private deployments we can configure customer-managed logging and KMS for key control. For Dedicated we keep audit trails and SAML SSO integrations. We'll attach the SOC2 and network diagram docs.
[06:03] Lena Ortiz: One more nuance: streaming protocols sometimes skip some perf markers for kernel times; ensure you enable server-side perf annotations during test runs.
[06:11] Aisha Khan: Ok that makes sense.
[06:13] Speaker 1: (soft) what about cost implications?
[06:15] Samir Patel: Dedicated pools cost more in fixed commit but reduce p99 by removing multi-tenant interference; we'll show cost/perf tradeoffs in the sheet. Also quantization reduces GPU cycles and thus cost per token.
[06:28] Ben Cho: Any quick wins to drop our p99 from 420ms to <250ms without a full dedicated purchase?
[06:34] Lena Ortiz: Yes: 1) enable prefix caching for top-50 flows, 2) raise micro-batch flush to 10ms for short flows and use priority routing for small sessions, 3) pre-warm critical prefixes at peak times, 4) reduce network hops (edge config). These usually cut p99 substantially.
[06:50] Aisha Khan: Great. Let's run the pilot. We'll pull session samples and Lena's config.
[06:56] Samir Patel: Awesome. We'll follow up with the sheet and schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-12-13.
[07:02] Ben Cho: Thanks everyone.
[07:05] (call ends)
